newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Mattel profits fall, hurt by strong dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mattel profits fall, hurt by strong dollar.

text.p: Toymaker Mattel Inc. Thursday reported lower first quarter earnings, reflecting the impact of a stronger dollar, costs related to its acquisition of Tyco Toys Inc. and a decline in sales at its Fisher-Price division.
Sales of Barbie, Mattel's most famous doll, were up 10 percent and sales of Disney products rose more than 20 percent. Hot Wheels sales nearly doubled, Mattel said.

"Tyco products were also in strong demand, with a sales increase of 27 percent led by the strength of the Tyco core brands of Sesame Street, Matchbox and Magna Doodle," said Mattel Chief Executive Jill Barad.
But sales of Fisher-Price toys fell 29 percent from a year earlier.

"It's going to be a difficult transition year for Mattel in the face of tough Barbie comparisons, the integration of Tyco Toys, a major restructuring at Mattel and a new management team," said Jill Krutick, analyst with Smith Barney.
Tyco Toys, which Mattel acquired in March, is the maker of last Christmas' hottest toy, Tickle Me Elmo.

Mattel reported earnings of $13 million, or 5 cents a share, for the 1997 first quarter, excluding a $275 million charge for the merger with Tyco and a restructuring at Mattel. A year ago, Mattel earned $29.9 million, or 11 cents a share, excluding one-time items.
Including the charge, Mattel posted a loss of $205 million, or 72 cents a share, in this year's first quarter.
First quarter net sales for Mattel, without the impact of Tyco sales, were $569 million, down 3 percent from $586 million in the year-ago quarter.

Mattel said the merger and the restructuring are expected to result in savings of $700 million over the next five years. In March, Mattel announced plans to lay off 2,700 employees as part of the restructuring.
Barad said the integration of Tyco operations and restructuring will result in pre-tax savings of $60 million this year and $160 million per year in 1998 and beyond.
Analysts said they believed cost-cutting efforts related to the integration of Tyco Toys and a turnaround at Fisher-Price will boost results later this year.

"Basically, they shipped too much Fisher-Price product last year and need to focus more on basic toys rather than items like outdoor equipment and electronic learning products," said Sean McGowan, analyst with Gerard Klauer Mattison.

McGowan said he expects to see another decline in Fisher-Price revenues in the second quarter, but that Fisher-Price shipments should begin to rise after that as retailers work through their inventories.
The current quarter's bottom line was also hurt by the strength of the dollar, which makes sales in foreign currencies worth less in dollar terms.

Mattel Thursday also named Harry Pearce to the position of chief financial officer, effective May 1, replacing Francesca Luzuriaga, who assumes the role of executive vice president-worldwide business planning and resources.
Pearce was chief financial officer of Tyco Toys before the merger.
Mattel has its headquarters in El Segundo, Calif., manufacturing facilities in 36 countries and sells its products in more than 140 nations throughout the world.
Mattel stock closed up $1.25 at $26.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
